items.stem: Use the unit circle to evaluate $\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$.
items.hint: Cosine is the $x$-coordinate of the terminal point, so settle which quadrant $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ lands in before you commit to a sign.
worked: $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=120^{\circ}$, which is in Quadrant II, so the reference angle is $\pi-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
The terminal point at $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ is $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$, so the reference value is $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
In Quadrant II the $x$-coordinate is negative, so $\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=-\dfrac{1}{2}$.

items.stem: Exactly one of the four statements below about the unit circle is true. Which one?
items.hint: Test each claim against an angle whose point you already know, such as $\theta=0$ or $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
worked: By definition the terminal side of $\theta$ meets the unit circle at $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$: the $x$-coordinate is cosine, the $y$-coordinate is sine.
At $\theta=0$ that point is $(1,0)$, so $\cos(0)=1$ and $\sin(0)=0$, exactly as the first statement says.

The others fail: $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$ because the point is $(0,1)$; $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ sits in Quadrant III where sine is negative, so $\sin\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$; and $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ radians is $30^{\circ}$, not half a degree.

options.text: The terminal side of $\theta$ meets the unit circle at $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$, so at $\theta=0$ the point is $(1,0)$.
The terminal side of $\theta$ meets the unit circle at $(\sin\theta,\cos\theta)$, so $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=1$.
The reference angle of $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so $\sin\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
Since $\dfrac{\pi}{6}\approx 0.52$, the angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ is about half a degree, so $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\approx 0$.

items.stem: The terminal point of $\theta$ on the unit circle lies in Quadrant IV and has $x$-coordinate $\dfrac{3}{5}$. A student writes $\sin\theta=\sqrt{1-\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^{2}}=1-\dfrac{3}{5}=\dfrac{2}{5}$. Her work contains two separate errors. What is the correct value of $\sin\theta$?
items.hint: Redo her radical step as one square root of the single number $1-\dfrac{9}{25}$, then let the quadrant choose the sign.
worked: Take the root of the whole quantity: $y=\pm\dfrac{4}{5}$. A radical never splits across a subtraction, so $\sqrt{1-\dfrac{9}{25}}\ne 1-\dfrac{3}{5}$.
In Quadrant IV the $y$-coordinate is negative, and sine is that $y$-coordinate, so $\sin\theta=-\dfrac{4}{5}$.

items.hint: The vertical line $x=-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ cuts the unit circle twice; count the crossings before writing anything down.
worked: Cosine is the $x$-coordinate, and $x$ is negative in Quadrants II and III, so there are two solutions.
Quadrant II gives $\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ and Quadrant III gives $\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{5\pi}{4}$.

items.stem: The terminal point of $\theta$ on the unit circle lies in Quadrant III and has $y$-coordinate $-\dfrac{1}{2}$. Find the exact value of $\tan\theta$.
items.hint: Recover the $x$-coordinate from $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$, sign it by the quadrant, then build the ratio $\dfrac{y}{x}$.
worked: In Quadrant III the $x$-coordinate is negative, so $x=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
